Created Hermit CRM, an open source CRM for 1 person. Hermit helps to keep track of deals and prospecting. raw.text:
Hi HN. I have potato computer. I tried running this flash game (N, the way of the ninja!) from 2004 (!), but my laptop from 2016 struggled to run it (yes, even with official Flashplayer!).

title: NariQ: BF16-level Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file
author: toebee

raw.text:
We built NariQ: 3-bit-or-lower quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B that retain near-BF16 quality across agentic tasks, math, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding.

To our knowledge, this is the first 3-bit-or-lower quantization that retains BF16 lvl performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.

Benchmarks (BF16 / 3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit):

- DeepSWE: 39.8 / 41.0 / 41.9 / 28.6

- Terminal-Bench 2.1: 62.6 / 63.8 / 60.2 / 52.4

- AIME 25+26: 97.7 / 98.3 / 96.5 / 86.0

- MSGM: 94.0 / 93.1 / 91.8 / 90.6

- RealWorldQA: 82.4 / 82.4 / 81.3 / 80.9

Decode speed is comparable to other quants on an RTX PRO 6000. Context-length results below

(3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit / Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS):

- 4K: 88.9 / 99.2 / 111.7 / 94.7

- 16K: 84.5 / 93.8 / 105.1 / 89.8

- 64K: 70.7 / 77.5 / 85.0 / 74.8

Running these currently require our llama.cpp fork: (https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp)

Feedback and questions welcome. We'd love to hear how these perform on your workloads.

title: Show HN: An interactive album that changes with stuff like time and moon phase
author: blouis

raw.text:
I've made Return to Repeat, an album and a browser music player with ten songs without beginning or end. It has built-in musical variations, some you can control and interact with and some that activate based on things like date, time of day, visit counts and current moon phase. Try the birds on track three for a starting place.

Wanted to explore other ways of releasing and experiencing digital music, and perhaps finding a route back to kind of "being" with music. My last release was a cassette in an edition of three, that also came with a minimal web player.

It's built mainly with Tone.js on the Web Audio API, with help from Claude (writing code, debugging). The music is composed as (sometimes long) seamless loops, with multiple stems for variations. Didn't want to go the proper app-route, with the main trade-off being no background audio. Also had some trouble with airplay, but think I've managed to get rid of the most obvious bugs.

Love to hear what you think of the listening experience! Happy to answer any questions about the project.

title: Show HN: I wrote FlightTrack twice
author: bkazez

raw.text:
FlightTrack was my iPhone flight tracker from the early App Store days (bestselling travel app for 4 years), and I just rewrote it from scratch.

I first wrote FlightTrack as a side project in 2008. It did really well and I quit my day job and started a company around it that was bought by Expedia in 2010; Expedia retired the app in 2017. By then I had burned out and focused my energy on classical singing, which turns out to mean living in airports. But I missed the app.

This summer I started rebuilding it from scratch, with a design inspired by Paul Mijksenaar's fantastic signage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, and working with Claude to write a server in Go and an iOS app in Swift. In 2008 v1.0 took me 6 weeks of evenings/weekends; now it took about the same amount of time, but thanks to Claude, I ended up with much more functionality (e.g. inbound flight tracking) and was able to try entire design iterations as functional code rather than just mockups.

The data is way more expensive now, so it’s a $59.99/yr subscription, but I’m giving a free year to the first 100 subscribers. I'll be adding lots of features soon but wanted to get this version out for Thanksgiving travel. Let me know anything you want and I'll do my best!

title: Show HN: PlaceBench – Testing AI on opening and closing hours (and last trains)
author: ymarkov

raw.text:
Hi everyone, we love maps and doing some fun side quests exploring this domain.

We were always surprised by the fact that products like ChatGpt recommends you places to go which have been shut down for years.

Last March we built a benchmark measuring how often LLMs make mistakes when answering places-based queries (e.g. Recommend me a restaurant in Marina for a dinner). Even with the web grounding (which is a very expensive tool relative to the token price), the results were not good - 1 out 10 places in the best model were made up or shut-down.

When personal assistants started to come up, we were curious to check how well they do with those queries. It turns out that much better, but they also take longer time to answer. We make it slightly more challenging, we made a benchmark a bit more sophisticated and measured it.

The best one turned out to be Dots from OpenAI, and it is also one of the fastest. The worst one was Grok Bot from XAI. We also measured Ask Maps from Google, but it was out of competition, because it is not technically a personal assistant. The more detailed results are available in the repository

title: Show HN: I built Maeto, an SRv6 SD-WAN from scratch on Linux that you can break
author: saphalpdyl

raw.text:
Demo: https://maeto.saphal.me/

GitHub (mirror): https://github.com/saphalpdyl/Maeto

Forgejo instance (issues & planning): https://git.saphal.me/saphalpdyl/Maeto

Small writeups about Maeto: https://blogs.saphal.me/tags/maeto/

---

About 5 months ago, I was tracking osvbng, a vBNG built on VPP. It was mentioned by folks on my previous Show HN, and I saw maintainers talk about Segment Routing support for it. Four months ago, I happened to be in a conversation about SD-WANs (Software-Defined WAN), and it got me thinking about Segment Routing again. So, I started Maeto that evening to learn about traffic engineering.

Maeto intends to be a complete SD-WAN platform: covering everything from the customer edge all the way up to the controller. It draws inspiration from Cato Networks and Google's B4. While initially designed to be a small complete lab, it exploded in scope as things got more and more interesting. And honestly, I'm having a blast.

I just finished implementing high availability (HA) and CE dual-homing. Locally, core detection runs at <50ms and CE (Customer Edge) detection runs at ~300ms (deliberate design since CE-PE edge over public internet). Though in the lab, you may see slightly higher numbers due to softirq saturation because of the random traffic being generated in the background.

Mostly written in Go. Frontend is Elixir Phoenix LiveView (live state is easier there), with C for FRR patches and Python for topology generation. The dashboard is laptop-sized; it's not usable on phones yet. While built with production circumstances in mind, it is far from being production-ready, and will remain a hobby project.

I've got classes and finals coming up. So, I'm presenting this early. I hope I'm allowed to post an update on it in 5-6 months when much cooler things are in place :D

---

Recommended simulation steps if YOU JUST WANNA SEE IT WORK:

- Ideally have 2 tabs of Maeto opened.

- In one of the tabs, go to Operations > Simulator. On stories, run the "PeSLC goes down" story.

- Watch the link-down detection, PLR indicators, and ping loss being <800ms.

---

Known limitations:

- It is emulated. Each node shares the same kernel performing multiple veth hops, encrypt/decrypt, encap/decap per-packet. So, the numbers are not representative and underestimate the performance if it were on dedicated hardware. Performance primarily tanks due to ksoftirq saturation.

- No internet breakout. So, it only supports site-site connections.

- TI-LFA is in the controller and is implemented in its most basic form (more in FAQ). - Only egress protection is implemented, and core P-P links are controller-protected, not local (more in FAQ).

A few questions:

- Maeto does color-based steering (SR policies), and polices bandwidth based on its color. Policing is harsh. It would be ideal for the CE to shape that traffic. This means the classification has to run in the CPE (it runs in PE today). It is just DSCP->color today, but in the future, we may want DPI to classify packets which are not marked. In that case, would it be reasonable to have DPI being done on the CPE which, from my understanding, are light low-compute boxes?

- How do operators tune BFD timers on edges that run on public internet transit (CE-PE edge)? I understand that static timers would be bad when propagation delay may vary. One way I can think of is observing a baseline delay and dynamically tuning BFD based on that?

I answer some of the questions readers may have at https://github.com/saphalpdyl/Maeto#faqs . I would appreciate comments, questions, answers, or feedback from people with operational experience or people who are just curious :)
